title: Negotiate well, talk across cultures, measure your results

say: Negotiate well, talk across cultures, and measure your results.
This is the video for module 4 of Business Communication.
Every business negotiates all the time: with suppliers on price, with landlords on rent, with customers on discounts.
Good negotiation is not shouting or tricks. It is mostly preparation, listening and clear communication.

say: And your BATNA, which means best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It is what you will do if there is no deal.
The stronger your alternative, the more confidently you can negotiate.

say: For example, Zainab makes dresses in Kaduna and pays about 9,000 naira per piece of Ankara. These prices are illustrative.
Her target is 8,200 and her walk-away is 8,600. Her alternative is another wholesaler who quoted 8,500, with slower delivery.

panel.heading: Zainab negotiates a fabric price
items: Prepare: target 8,200, walk away at 8,600
Open: 50 pieces a month at 8,000?
Listen: what would help you most?
Trade: full payment on collection
Agree at 8,300 and confirm in writing

say: She opens: I plan to order 50 pieces every month instead of 20. Could you do 8,000 per piece?

say: The wholesaler says that is too low. Zainab asks, what would help you most? He says payment on time and fewer small orders.
That is his interest. His position was the price. His interest is reliable payment.

say: So she offers to pay in full on collection and order once a month.

say: They settle at 8,300 naira. That saves her 35,000 naira a month on 50 pieces.
She sends a WhatsApp summary of the deal the same day.

say: Notice that Zainab traded something for every step down in price. A common mistake is giving a discount and asking nothing in return.

panel.rule: Trade concessions. Never give a discount for nothing.

say: In high-context settings, much of the meaning is in the relationship and what is not said. Many West African business settings lean this way.
In low-context settings, people expect meaning in the words themselves. Neither is better. These are tendencies, not rules about every person.
So if a partner says, we will try our best, ask gently: should I plan for Friday or the following week? And with second-language readers, use short sentences and no slang like no wahala.
For example, Chiamaka exports shea butter from Abuja and needs a call with a buyer in New York. Nigeria uses West Africa Time, W A T.

Pick an overlap: 3pm WAT is 9am New York
State both times, check a world clock app

say: For your capstone, keep a communication log: a simple table where you record important messages and what happened.

cards.d: Date, who, channel, purpose, reply or not, days to reply, and follow-up questions.
Replies divided by important messages sent. It should rise as your writing improves.
Replies that asked for something your message should have said. It should fall.

say: Your response rate is the replies divided by the messages sent. For example, Ruth runs a cleaning service in Lagos. Before the course, 11 of her 20 messages got replies, 55%. After, 16 of 20, that is 80%.

cards.d: Date, who, channel, purpose, reply or not, days to reply, and follow-up questions.
Replies divided by important messages sent. It should rise as your writing improves.
Replies that asked for something your message should have said. It should fall.

say: Your clarification rate counts replies asking for missing details. Ruth's fell from about 55% to about 19%. That is honest evidence she can show a client or programme officer.

say: To remember. Prepare your numbers and your alternative. Look for the interest behind the position. Confirm every deal in writing.
Adjust to your reader, and state both times for calls abroad. And measure your messages, so you have real evidence.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Prepare target, walk-away, opening offer and BATNA
Look for the interest behind every position
End every negotiation with a written summary
Adjust style to your reader; state both times
Track response and clarification rates
